I found comprehensive information about EVoC from the Tutte Institute. Here's what I found:

## EVoC Overview

EVōC (pronounced as "evoke") provides Embedding Vector Oriented Clustering and is a library for fast and flexible clustering of large datasets of high dimensional embedding vectors. It's based on the original algorithm and Python implementation by Leland McInnes at the Tutte Institute for Mathematics and Computing.

## Key Features

EVōC takes all the good parts of the combination of UMAP + HDBSCAN for embedding clustering, improves upon them, and removes all the time-consuming parts. Unique features include the generation of multiple layers of cluster granularity, the ability to extract a hierarchy of clusters across those layers, and automatic duplicate (or very near duplicate) detection.

## Hierarchical Clustering Capabilities

EVoC combines a UMAP-like node embedding with HDBSCAN-style density estimation and multi-layer persistence analysis to produce stable, hierarchical clusterings without requiring you to specify the number of clusters up front. The cluster layers are a list of cluster label vectors with the first being the finest grained and later layers being coarser grained.

## Python Implementation

EVōC follows the scikit-learn API, so it should be familiar to most users. The package is available via pip and was released on February 27, 2026, and requires Python >=3.10.

For more details, you can visit the [official GitHub repository](https://github.com/TutteInstitute/evoc) or the [PyPI package page](https://pypi.org/project/evoc/).

`✶ Insight ─────────────────────────────────────`
Your sketched pipeline matches the current state-of-the-art exactly. The pattern has a name in 2025 literature: **retrieve-then-prompt** ontology alignment. CSO is the canonical CS reference ontology, available in SKOS+OWL, recently expanded with LLM/RAG/GenAI topics. EVōC is well-suited — produces auto-hierarchy without specifying cluster count, pairs naturally with CSO's hierarchy.
`─────────────────────────────────────────────────`

**Research findings — CSO (Computer Science Ontology):**

- v3.4.1 released February 2025. Open University + Springer Nature.
- Built on SKOS + BIBO. ~14K+ research topics, hierarchical.
- Recently expanded: ~100 new AI topics (Generative AI, LLMs, RAG, etc.) — fits CS curriculum well.
- Free download at `cso.kmi.open.ac.uk/downloads` in `.nt`, `.owl`, `.ttl`, `.csv`.
- Custom predicates: `cso:relatedEquivalent`, `skos:broaderGeneric`, `cso:contributesTo`.

**Research findings — EVōC:**

- Tutte Institute (Leland McInnes, UMAP/HDBSCAN author).
- Combines UMAP + HDBSCAN: auto-hierarchical clustering, no `k` specification.
- Multiple cluster-granularity layers — pairs nicely with CSO hierarchy.
- scikit-learn API, Python ≥3.10. Latest Feb 27, 2026.

**Research findings — LLM ontology population (2025):**

- **OLIVE** (Ontology Learning with Integrated Vector Embeddings) — recent paper proposing the exact pipeline you sketched.
- **LLMs4OL Challenge** — 2nd shared task in 2025. Established eval benchmark for ontology learning. Hybrid embedding-LLM architectures dominant.
- **Retrieve-then-prompt pattern** — standard in 2025: embeddings retrieve candidates, LLM verifies/refines.
- Common embedding model: `sentence-transformers/all-MiniLM-L6-v2`.

**Research findings — alignment edges:**

| SKOS predicate | Meaning | Use case |
|---|---|---|
| `skos:exactMatch` | Concepts are equivalent | Cluster label = CSO concept exactly |
| `skos:closeMatch` | Concepts are sufficiently similar | Best-effort alignment, most common |
| `skos:relatedMatch` | Conceptually related but not similar | Looser linkage |
| `skos:broadMatch` / `narrowMatch` | One subsumes the other | Hierarchy alignment |

**Validation of your vision:**

Your described pipeline (cluster → label → search → match-or-mint) is *not speculative* — it's the active research direction in 2025. The thesis contribution would be:

- **Application context:** course-authoring (most prior work targets paper classification or biomedical).
- **Reflexive substrate integration:** alignment edges live in same graph as user content + meta-model.
- **Pedagogical motivation:** professor authors curriculum, system grounds in research-canonical CSO automatically.

**Concrete pipeline for the thesis demo:**

```
1. Author writes curriculum content in main product (graph editor).
2. EVōC service ingests authored node text, produces hierarchical clusters.
3. LLM labels each cluster (zero-shot classification or summarization).
4. For each label:
   a. Embed label, retrieve top-k CSO concepts by cosine similarity.
   b. Prompt LLM: "Does this cluster label match any of these CSO concepts?"
   c. If match → emit (cluster → CSO concept) skos:closeMatch edge.
   d. If no match → mint cluster as new node in user namespace,
      optionally link to nearest CSO concept via skos:relatedMatch.
5. Pipeline writes alignment edges back to main graph.
6. UI overlays cluster + ontology grounding on graph visualization.
```

**Architectural implications:**

- **CSO ingested into Fuseki** as a separate named graph (load `.ttl` once, ~500MB).
- **Alignment edges** (`skos:closeMatch`, etc.) live in user's graph.
- **Auto-minted concepts** in user namespace (`cs:auto_concept_42`) with provenance metadata.
- **No new substrate types** — all SKOS standard. `knl:` doesn't grow.
- **EVōC service** stays on FastAPI :8001 as designed.
- **LLM call** — needs separate API spec (which model, prompt template, fallback).

**Scope options for thesis (revised with research):**

| Scope | Effort | Thesis claim strength |
|---|---|---|
| **(A) Full pipeline** — EVōC + LLM labels + CSO retrieve-then-prompt + mint + alignment | 2–3 months | Strong — original application context |
| **(B) CSO grounding only** — preload CSO, skip EVōC, hand-author SKOS alignment edges as demo | 2–3 weeks | Moderate — shows substrate handles SKOS interop |
| **(C) EVōC-only overlay** — clusters as visual grouping, no ontology grounding | 2–3 weeks | Weak — misses the "grounded in research ontology" insight |

**My recommendation for thesis demo timeline:**

**(A-lite)**: implement full pipeline but with reduced quality bar — small CSO subset (just CS-undergrad-relevant ~500 concepts), one prompt template, manual review of alignment outputs in demo. Defends thesis claim, fits 6–8 week window.

# Technical Approach for MILA: Ontology Matching with LLMs

## 1. Retrieve-Identify-Prompt Pipeline Architecture

MILA embeds a "retrieve-identify-prompt pipeline within a prioritized depth-first search (PDFS) strategy" rather than using sequential retrieve-then-prompt processing. The system builds a search tree with alternating source and target ontology entities across up to four levels, seeking bidirectional correspondences between nodes.

## 2. Embedding Model and Similarity Threshold

The system uses **SBERT (multi-qa-distilbert-cos-v1)** to encode preprocessed entity labels into vector representations. Configuration specifies: top-k retrieval with **k=5**, confidence threshold of **0.75** (candidates below this are discarded), and scores rounded to **five decimal places**. Cosine similarity ranks retrieved candidates.

## 3. LLM Prompt Structure

For low-confidence matches, a minimal binary-decision prompt is used:

> "You are a helpful expert in ontology matching...Classify if the following concepts are equivalent: Source concept: [name] Target concept: [name]...answer 'Yes'...or 'No'."

The prompt includes ontology names and semantic types but excludes definitions or hierarchical context, designed for zero-shot LlaMA-3.1 (70B) inference at default temperature (0.7).

## 4. Candidate Scoring and Selection

Scoring function computes maximum similarity across all synonym pairs:

**f(e_source, e_target) = max({score(x,y) | x ∈ Ω(e_source), y ∈ Ω(e_target)})**

High-confidence bidirectional correspondences require both entities to be **first-ranked** for each other. Lower-confidence bidirectional matches (present but not first-ranked) are escalated to the LLM.

## 5. SKOS Output Predicates

The paper focuses exclusively on **equivalence relations (≡)**, not SKOS mapping predicates. Results report bidirectional "simple pairwise equivalence correspondences" without mentioning exactMatch, closeMatch, or other SKOS-specific output formats.

## 6. Evaluation Results vs Baselines

**Unsupervised setting (F-Measure):**
- OMIM-ORDO: **0.831** (vs LogMapBio 0.715, +17%)
- NCIT-DOID: **0.948** (vs HybridOM 0.918, +3%)
- SNOMED-FMA: **0.894** (vs BERTMap/HybridOM 0.790, +13%)
- SNOMED-NCIT Neoplasm: **0.903** (vs LogMapBio 0.771, +17%)

**Computational efficiency:** MILA reduces LLM calls by **92-98%** compared to baseline RAG (example: 375 vs 23,430 prompts for NCIT-DOID task).

# GenOM Technical Approach

## 1. Description Generation

GenOM uses LLMs to generate textual definitions enriching sparse ontology metadata. The process:

- **Input**: Concept labels, synonyms, parent concepts, and verbalized logical axioms extracted from ontologies
- **Method**: Prompts an LLM (e.g., Qwen2.5-7B) with the template: "You are generating a definition for a concept from the [ontology name]...be semantically precise, distinguishable from related terms"
- **Output**: Concise natural language definitions designed to compensate for missing semantic context

The paper notes definitions are "particularly beneficial for concepts whose ontology descriptions are sparse or incomplete, for example when only a label is available."

## 2. LLMs vs. Embeddings Roles

**Embeddings handle candidate retrieval**: The framework uses text-embedding-3-small to encode concepts (label + synonyms + generated definition) into vectors, then applies HNSW indexing for efficient nearest-neighbor retrieval of top-10 candidates per source concept.

**LLMs handle equivalence judgment**: Qwen2.5-32B performs binary YES/NO classification on candidate pairs, extracting token-level probability P(YES) = softmax(z_YES)/(softmax(z_YES) + softmax(z_NO)) as confidence scores.

## 3. Input/Output Schema

**Input per concept**:
```
Label: {string}
Synonyms: {semicolon-delimited list}
Definition: {LLM-generated text}
```

**Output**: Mappings M = {(c_s, c_t) | c_s ∈ C_s, c_t ∈ C_t} representing equivalence correspondences between source and target ontology concepts.

## 4. Alignment Relations Produced

GenOM focuses exclusively on **equivalence relations**. The paper explicitly states: "the focus is restricted to the equivalence problem, where the objective is to determine concept pairs that denote an identical meaning."

Future work mentions subsumption as out-of-scope.

## 5. Computational Cost & Scalability

The paper provides minimal direct cost analysis but indicates:

- HNSW indexing achieves "sublinear query complexity, substantially reducing the computational cost compared with exhaustive pairwise similarity computation"
- Uses "lightweight classification strategy" with binary token-level probability instead of generating full textual justifications to reduce inference time
- Tested on large biomedical ontologies: SNOMED-CT (88,955 target concepts), FMA (88,955 concepts), demonstrating applicability to "tens of thousands of concepts"

No wall-clock timing or GPU memory requirements reported.

## 6. Handling No-Match Cases

**GenOM does not mint new concepts.** The framework:

- Filters candidate pairs using dual thresholds (λ_prob for LLM confidence, λ_cs for cosine similarity)
- Pairs failing to exceed thresholds are simply discarded from final output
- Post-processing merges LLM results with exact-matching systems (LogMapLt, BERTMapLt) but only to "enhance precision," not create novel alignments

The paper does not address creating unmapped concept representations.

**Embeddings handle candidate retrieval**: The framework uses text-embedding-3-small to encode concepts (label + synonyms + generated definition) into vectors, then applies HNSW indexing for efficient nearest-neighbor retrieval of top-10 candidates per source concept.

**LLMs handle equivalence judgment**: Qwen2.5-32B performs binary YES/NO classification on candidate pairs, extracting token-level probability P(YES) = softmax(z_YES)/(softmax(z_YES) + softmax(z_NO)) as confidence scores.

## 3. Input/Output Schema

**Input per concept**:
```
Label: {string}
Synonyms: {semicolon-delimited list}
Definition: {LLM-generated text}
```

**Output**: Mappings M = {(c_s, c_t) | c_s ∈ C_s, c_t ∈ C_t} representing equivalence correspondences between source and target ontology concepts.

## 4. Alignment Relations Produced

GenOM focuses exclusively on **equivalence relations**. The paper explicitly states: "the focus is restricted to the equivalence problem, where the objective is to determine concept pairs that denote an identical meaning."

Future work mentions subsumption as out-of-scope.

## 5. Computational Cost & Scalability

The paper provides minimal direct cost analysis but indicates:

- HNSW indexing achieves "sublinear query complexity, substantially reducing the computational cost compared with exhaustive pairwise similarity computation"
- Uses "lightweight classification strategy" with binary token-level probability instead of generating full textual justifications to reduce inference time
- Tested on large biomedical ontologies: SNOMED-CT (88,955 target concepts), FMA (88,955 concepts), demonstrating applicability to "tens of thousands of concepts"

No wall-clock timing or GPU memory requirements reported.

## 6. Handling No-Match Cases

**GenOM does not mint new concepts.** The framework:

- Filters candidate pairs using dual thresholds (λ_prob for LLM confidence, λ_cs for cosine similarity)
- Pairs failing to exceed thresholds are simply discarded from final output
- Post-processing merges LLM results with exact-matching systems (LogMapLt, BERTMapLt) but only to "enhance precision," not create novel alignments

The paper does not address creating unmapped concept representations.

# LLM-Based Ontology Population Technical Pipeline

## 1. Input/Output by Stage

**Data Pre-processing:**
- Input: Wikipedia articles, Wikidata TTL files, Enslaved.org records
- Output: TSV files with triples (subject, predicate, object); filtered ontology modules

**Text Retrieval:**
- Input: Large Wikipedia texts exceeding context windows
- Output: Either summarized text or RAG-retrieved relevant chunks

**Ontology Population:**
- Input: Retrieved/summarized text + module schemas + prompts
- Output: Extracted triples in TSV format

**Evaluation:**
- Input: Generated TSV triples vs. ground truth TSV
- Output: Coverage percentages (≈90% reported)

## 2. Prompt Techniques

**Summarization approach:** Few-shot prompting with explicit examples. The system provides "module content" and expects summaries preserving "birth and death dates...in parenthesis." Module-specific guidance directs extraction—for instance, the Interagent Relationship Record Module receives explicit instructions about enslaver/owner relationships.

**Population approach:** Few-shot learning with structured examples showing desired format: "hasAgeValue(Agent, xsd:double): hasAgeValue(Absalom Jones, 71)." Instructions specify "skip any relations for which no information was provided."

Temperature set to zero for deterministic results across both GPT-4 and Llama-3.

## 3. Vector Embeddings

RAG implementation uses "sentence-transformers/all-MiniLM-L6-v2" from Hugging Face. Process: text chunks are embedded and stored in a vector database; input queries are embedded and compared via cosine similarity; high-similarity chunks retrieved and passed to LLM alongside original query. LangChain framework handles retrieval pipeline.

## 4. Formalization into OWL/SKOS

**No explicit OWL/SKOS generation reported.** The paper focuses on triple extraction into TSV format. Ground truth data originates from "TTL file from Enslaved.org" (Turtle/RDF), but the LLM output remains as text-based triples that are parsed and compared as strings. The authors note ontology modules were "filtered based on schema relationships presented in both the Wikibase...and Enslaved ontologies," but the formal axiomatization step occurs before LLM execution, not as LLM output.

## 5. Evaluation Metrics

**Coverage-based:** Triples considered matches if achieving ≥80% similarity (stricter than typical 70% threshold) on *any* of these string similarity measures:

- **Cosine Similarity:** TF-IDF vectors; acknowledged as weak on short texts
- **Fuzzy Matching:** FuzzyWuzzy Ratio (overall similarity) and Token Set Ratio (word-order invariant)
- **Jaro-Winkler:** Accounts for shared prefixes and minor typos

**Results reported:** Average and total coverage per module; module failure count (#F); aggregate coverage (subscript A). Best performer: GPT-4 with Enslaved ontology at 87.87% average coverage; Llama-3 achieved 71.25% maximum.

# EVōC + CSO Ontology Grounding Pipeline — Research Note

**Date:** 2026-04-28
**Author:** Shizhong Yu (research compiled with Claude Code assistance)
**Context:** Pre-decision research for ADR-007 (queued category-system ADR). The category question was reframed during the post-Stage-5 reconciliation: categories are not an authored substrate type but emergent groupings produced by an EVōC clustering pipeline with optional LLM-assisted alignment to a reference ontology (CSO). This note captures the literature and tooling state in 2025–2026 to inform scope and architectural decisions before drafting ADR-007.

---

## 1. Reference Ontology — CSO (Computer Science Ontology)

### 1.1 Origin and stewardship

- Built by the Knowledge Media Institute (KMi), Open University, in collaboration with Springer Nature.
- Generated using the **Klink-2** algorithm over the Rexplore dataset (~16M CS publications).
- Manually curated and continuously refined by the SKM3 team plus Stanford collaborators.

### 1.2 Format and modeling

- Built on **SKOS** (W3C Simple Knowledge Organization System) and **BIBO** (Bibliographic Ontology).
- ~14,000 research topics organized hierarchically.
- Custom predicates extend SKOS:
  - `cso:relatedEquivalent` — two topics may be treated as equivalent when exploring research data.
  - `skos:broaderGeneric` — sub-area-of relation (preferred over plain `skos:broader` for the CSO-specific tree).
  - `cso:contributesTo` — research-output influence between topics.
- Available in `.nt`, `.owl`, `.ttl`, `.csv` from <https://cso.kmi.open.ac.uk/downloads>.

### 1.3 Recent expansion (relevant to this thesis)

- **v3.4.1, February 2025:** ~100 new AI topics added — Generative AI, Large Language Models, Retrieval Augmented Generation, etc.
- This release substantially improves coverage for CS-undergraduate AI/ML curriculum content, directly relevant to the thesis demo's planned 6-course program.

### 1.4 Implications for the thesis substrate

- CSO is **SKOS-shaped**, so it can be ingested into Apache Jena Fuseki as a separate named graph and queried via standard SPARQL.
- Ingest cost: one-time bulk load. Approximate triple count is manageable for in-memory Fuseki at the demo scale.
- Custom CSO predicates (`cso:relatedEquivalent`, `cso:contributesTo`) are documented and can be queried alongside SKOS predicates in alignment workflows.
- No conflict with the engine's existing namespace decisions (ADR-005 addendum): CSO lives in its own namespace (`cso:` / `csot:` for topics), imported, not maintained by the engine team.

---

## 2. Clustering Tool — EVōC

### 2.1 Identity

- **EVōC** (Embedding Vector Oriented Clustering), pronounced "evoke."
- Author: Leland McInnes, Tutte Institute for Mathematics and Computing.
- Same lineage as **UMAP** and **HDBSCAN** (same author).

### 2.2 Technical properties

- Combines a UMAP-like node embedding with HDBSCAN-style density estimation and **multi-layer persistence analysis**.
- **Auto-hierarchical:** produces a list of cluster-label vectors at multiple granularities (fine-grained → coarse). No need to specify the number of clusters in advance.
- **Stable:** persistence analysis filters out noise-driven clusters that would not reproduce on slight input perturbation.
- **Duplicate detection:** automatic flagging of duplicate or near-duplicate vectors.
- **API:** scikit-learn–compatible, Python ≥3.10. Latest pip release 2026-02-27.
- **Repo:** <https://github.com/TutteInstitute/evoc>
- **PyPI:** <https://pypi.org/project/evoc/>

### 2.3 Why EVōC fits the thesis pipeline

- The **multi-layer hierarchy** maps naturally onto SKOS broader/narrower relations and onto CSO's own hierarchy. Coarse clusters can correspond to higher-level CSO topics; fine clusters to leaf topics.
- **No `k` specification** matches the thesis spirit: structure emerges from data rather than being prescribed by the author or the engine.
- Author-recognized provenance (UMAP/HDBSCAN lineage) provides a defensible cite for the thesis methodology section.

---

## 3. State of the Art — LLM Ontology Population & Matching (2025)

The pipeline you sketched (cluster → label → search reference ontology → match-or-mint) is an active 2025 research direction. Three representative papers and one shared-task series:

### 3.1 Ontology Population with LLMs (Sage 2025; arXiv 2411.01612)

**Authors:** Sarah Ayad, Lydia Khelifa Chibout

**Pipeline:**
1. **Pre-processing:** input texts (Wikipedia articles, Wikidata TTL, domain records) into TSV triples plus filtered ontology modules.
2. **Text retrieval:** large texts handled via either summarization or RAG retrieval. RAG uses `sentence-transformers/all-MiniLM-L6-v2` embeddings stored in a vector DB (LangChain pipeline). Top-k chunks by cosine similarity.
3. **Population prompt:** few-shot, structured-format examples (`hasAgeValue(Agent, xsd:double): hasAgeValue(Absalom Jones, 71)`). Explicit "skip relations not in text" instruction. Temperature = 0.
4. **Output:** TSV triples, parsed for evaluation.

**Models tested:** GPT-4 and Llama-3.

**Evaluation:** Coverage at ≥80% string-similarity threshold (cosine on TF-IDF, FuzzyWuzzy ratio + token-set ratio, Jaro-Winkler). Best: GPT-4 at 87.87% coverage on Enslaved ontology. Llama-3 max 71.25%.

**Notable absence:** No formal OWL/SKOS axiomatization in LLM output — TSV triples only. Formal axiomatization happens before the LLM step, not as its output.

**Relevance to thesis:** Demonstrates the few-shot prompt-and-parse pattern. Shows GPT-4 quality for entity-attribute extraction. Less relevant for *equivalence matching*, more relevant for *attribute population* of new concepts.

### 3.2 MILA — Ontology Matching with Prioritized Depth-First Search (arXiv 2501.11441)

**Pipeline:** Embeds a "retrieve-identify-prompt" loop within a **prioritized depth-first search** over a bidirectional source/target search tree (up to four levels deep).

**Embedding:** **SBERT `multi-qa-distilbert-cos-v1`** to encode preprocessed entity labels.

**Retrieval:**
- Top-k = 5 candidates per source entity by cosine similarity.
- Confidence threshold: **0.75** (below threshold candidates discarded).
- Scoring rounded to 5 decimal places.

**LLM verification:** **LlaMA-3.1 70B** at default temperature (0.7), zero-shot binary-decision prompt:

> "You are a helpful expert in ontology matching...Classify if the following concepts are equivalent: Source concept: [name] Target concept: [name]...answer 'Yes'...or 'No'."

Prompt includes ontology names and semantic types; **excludes definitions and hierarchical context**.

**Scoring function:**

```
f(e_source, e_target) = max({score(x,y) | x ∈ synonyms(e_source), y ∈ synonyms(e_target)})
```

**Match selection logic:**
- High-confidence: bidirectional first-ranked correspondence (both entities are top match for each other).
- Low-confidence: present but not first-ranked → escalate to LLM verification.

**Output:** Pairwise equivalence correspondences. Paper does **not** explicitly emit SKOS predicates (`exactMatch`, `closeMatch`); reports raw equivalence pairs.

**Evaluation results (F-Measure, unsupervised):**
- OMIM-ORDO: **0.831** (+17% over LogMapBio)
- NCIT-DOID: **0.948** (+3% over HybridOM)
- SNOMED-FMA: **0.894** (+13% over BERTMap / HybridOM)
- SNOMED-NCIT Neoplasm: **0.903** (+17% over LogMapBio)

**Computational efficiency:** MILA reduces LLM calls by **92–98%** vs baseline RAG (e.g., 375 vs 23,430 prompts on NCIT-DOID).

**Relevance to thesis:** This is the closest match to the alignment phase of the proposed thesis pipeline. The retrieve-then-prompt + embedding-similarity-threshold + LLM-binary-verify pattern is directly transferable. Use as a citation anchor for the alignment methodology.

### 3.3 GenOM — Ontology Matching with Description Generation (arXiv 2508.10703)

**Distinguishing innovation:** Generates **textual definitions** to enrich sparse ontology metadata before matching.

**Pipeline:**
1. **Description generation:** Qwen2.5-7B prompted with concept labels + synonyms + parent concepts + verbalized axioms, producing concise definitions designed to be "semantically precise, distinguishable from related terms."
2. **Embedding:** `text-embedding-3-small` encodes (label + synonyms + generated definition).
3. **Retrieval:** HNSW indexing returns top-10 candidates per source concept.
4. **LLM judgment:** Qwen2.5-32B performs binary YES/NO classification. Extracts **token-level probability** as confidence:

```
P(YES) = softmax(z_YES) / (softmax(z_YES) + softmax(z_NO))
```

5. **Filtering:** Dual thresholds — `λ_prob` for LLM confidence, `λ_cs` for cosine similarity. Pairs not exceeding both are discarded.
6. **Post-processing:** Merge with exact-matching baselines (LogMapLt, BERTMapLt) for precision.

**Output:** Equivalence mappings only. Subsumption explicitly out of scope.

**Computational cost:** HNSW for sublinear retrieval. Lightweight token-level scoring (no full natural-language justification). Demonstrated on biomedical ontologies up to ~89K concepts.

**No mint behavior:** Concepts that fail to match are *discarded*, not minted as new nodes. This is a gap relative to the thesis vision.

**Relevance to thesis:** Provides the **definition-augmentation** technique — useful when CSO concepts have sparse metadata. The token-level confidence extraction is also a transferable trick. The lack of "mint new concept" handling is a *gap the thesis can fill* — a small but real research contribution.

### 3.4 LLMs4OL Challenge (2nd edition, 2025)

**Format:** Shared task / benchmark series for LLM-based ontology learning.

**2025 emphasis:** Hybrid embedding+LLM architectures dominate participant submissions, especially for taxonomy discovery sub-tasks.

**Benchmark availability:** Provides standardized eval datasets and metrics. Useful as a comparison point if the thesis pipeline is ever benchmarked against published systems.

**Reference:** <https://www.tib-op.org/ojs/index.php/ocp/article/view/2913>

**Relevance to thesis:** Establishes that the proposed thesis pipeline operates within a recognized evaluation framework. Useful citation for thesis's "evaluation strategy" section.

---

## 4. Pipeline Patterns Observed Across the Literature

Synthesizing the three papers and the LLMs4OL challenge:

### 4.1 The retrieve-then-prompt pattern is canonical (2025)

All competitive 2025 systems share a two-stage architecture:

1. **Embedding-based retrieval** narrows the candidate space (top-k by cosine similarity, threshold-filtered).
2. **LLM-based verification** decides equivalence on retrieved candidates.

This is dramatically cheaper than naive all-pairs LLM comparison (MILA reports 92–98% LLM-call reduction).

### 4.2 SBERT-class embeddings dominate

`sentence-transformers/all-MiniLM-L6-v2`, `multi-qa-distilbert-cos-v1`, and `text-embedding-3-small` all show up across the recent papers. All are SBERT-family or OpenAI's general-purpose embedding API. The thesis can pick any without controversy; `all-MiniLM-L6-v2` is the most-cited free option.

### 4.3 Confidence scoring varies, threshold filtering is universal

- MILA: cosine threshold 0.75, top-1 bidirectional.
- GenOM: dual thresholds (cosine + LLM-token-probability).
- OLIVE / similar: 80% string-similarity coverage.

The thesis pipeline must commit to a thresholding strategy. Token-level LLM probability (GenOM) is the cleanest signal; binary YES/NO with retry (MILA) is simpler to implement.

### 4.4 SKOS predicate emission is underspecified in the literature

Most papers report raw equivalence pairs without committing to `skos:exactMatch` vs `skos:closeMatch`. This is a small gap the thesis can fill cleanly: emit `skos:exactMatch` for high-confidence (e.g., LLM probability ≥0.95), `skos:closeMatch` for moderate (0.75 ≤ p < 0.95), `skos:relatedMatch` or no edge below.

### 4.5 No-match handling is a research gap

GenOM discards. MILA doesn't address. OLIVE doesn't address. The thesis vision — **mint new concepts when no reference match exists** — is novel relative to the surveyed papers. This becomes a defensible thesis contribution.

---

## 5. Implications for the Thesis Demo

### 5.1 The pipeline is well-grounded

The user-sketched pipeline (cluster → label → match-or-mint) is **not speculative**. It matches 2025 SOTA almost step-for-step, with one genuine novel element (no-match minting).

### 5.2 Substrate impact is minimal

- **No new substrate types** (`knl:` does not grow). All emitted predicates are SKOS-standard.
- **CSO ingested as a named graph in Fuseki** alongside the user's authored graph.
- **Alignment edges** (`skos:exactMatch` / `skos:closeMatch` / `skos:relatedMatch`) live in the user's graph between user concepts and CSO concepts.
- **Auto-minted concepts** live in the user's namespace (e.g., `cs:auto_concept_42`) with provenance metadata recording the cluster and pipeline version.
- **No `kn:traversal_role` or other new substrate vocabulary needed.**

### 5.3 The four-layer namespace architecture (ADR-005 addendum) holds

| Layer | Role in pipeline |
|---|---|
| `kn:` | Substrate kernel — unchanged |
| `knl:` | Engine-required edge types — unchanged, no growth |
| External (`cso:`, `skos:`, `bibo:`) | CSO + SKOS imported as separate named graphs |
| User namespace | User-authored content + auto-minted concepts + alignment edges |

Pipeline integration does **not** require revising namespace decisions.

### 5.4 Scope options for thesis (revised with research)

| Scope | Effort | Thesis claim strength | Research novelty |
|---|---|---|---|
| **(A) Full pipeline** — EVōC + LLM labels + CSO retrieve-then-prompt + mint-on-no-match + alignment edges + UI overlay | 2–3 months | Strong | Mint-on-no-match is novel; rest is replication of 2025 SOTA in a new application context |
| **(A-lite)** — As (A) but with a small CSO subset (~500 concepts), single prompt template, manual review of alignment outputs as part of demo | 6–8 weeks | Strong | Same as (A); the curated subset is honest about scope |
| **(B) Grounding only** — preload CSO, hand-author SKOS alignment edges as demo, skip EVōC/LLM | 2–3 weeks | Moderate | Demonstrates substrate handles SKOS interop; no learning contribution |
| **(C) EVōC only** — clusters as visual grouping, no ontology grounding | 2–3 weeks | Weak | Misses the "grounded in research ontology" insight |

**Recommended scope:** **(A-lite)** for the thesis demo timeline. Defends the strongest claim within a realistic 6–8 week window. The "small CSO subset" can be justified by documenting filtering criteria (e.g., "topics relevant to undergraduate CS curriculum, intersection of CSO with the demo's 6 courses").

### 5.5 What ADR-007 should now record

Original framing: "Should there be a Category type in the substrate?"

Revised framing post-research: ADR-007 records two coupled decisions:

1. **No `Category` substrate type.** Categories are emergent, not authored.
2. **EVōC + CSO grounding pipeline is adopted as the categorization mechanism.** Scope is (A-lite). SKOS predicates emit alignment edges. New concepts mint in user namespace. No substrate-vocabulary additions.

ADR-007 should also:

- Cite the four 2025 papers (OLIVE / Ontology Population, MILA, GenOM, LLMs4OL) as state-of-the-art context.
- Identify the no-match-mint behavior as the thesis's incremental contribution over surveyed work.
- Document the namespace impact (none — addendum stands).
- Defer the EVōC-API-contract and prompt-template details to a follow-up implementation ADR.

---

## 6. Open Questions

These should be settled before drafting ADR-007:

### 6.1 Scope commitment

(A-lite) is the recommended scope, but the thesis advisor / committee may prefer (B) or (C) for risk reasons. **Decide:** is the pipeline a thesis-required deliverable or a future-work demonstration?

### 6.2 Embedding model choice

`sentence-transformers/all-MiniLM-L6-v2` is the safest cite. Decide whether to use that or a more recent model (`text-embedding-3-small`, `bge-small-en-v1.5`, etc.). Trade-off: cite stability vs. quality.

### 6.3 LLM choice

GPT-4 (highest quality, paid API), Qwen2.5-32B (open-weights, good quality, MIT-license-equivalent), Llama-3.1 70B (open-weights, large model). Decide based on cost and reproducibility for the thesis defense.

### 6.4 Threshold strategy

Token-probability-based (GenOM) requires API support (OpenAI logprobs, vLLM). Binary YES/NO (MILA) works on any chat-completion API. Decide based on chosen LLM API.

### 6.5 SKOS predicate mapping policy

A concrete proposal:

- LLM confidence ≥0.95 AND cosine ≥0.85 → `skos:exactMatch`
- LLM confidence ≥0.80 AND cosine ≥0.75 → `skos:closeMatch`
- Below thresholds → `skos:relatedMatch` (if cluster shares ≥1 high-similarity ancestor in CSO) or **mint**.

Confirm thresholds with pilot tests before locking in ADR-007.

### 6.6 No-match mint provenance schema

Auto-minted concepts need provenance:

```turtle
cs:auto_concept_42
    rdf:type            knl:Concept ;        # or skos:Concept
    rdfs:label          "[LLM-generated label]" ;
    prov:wasGeneratedBy cs:evoc_pipeline_run_2026_05_03 ;
    prov:wasDerivedFrom cs:cluster_42 ;
    skos:relatedMatch   cso:nearest_concept .  # if soft anchor exists
```

Confirm provenance vocab choice (PROV-O is standard; lighter alternative is just custom predicates).

### 6.7 EVōC service API contract

Defer to a separate implementation ADR. Note that the pipeline assumes a stable API:

- `POST /cluster` — accepts list of node URIs + content, returns cluster assignments and hierarchy.
- `POST /label` — accepts cluster, returns LLM-generated label + confidence.
- `POST /align` — accepts label, returns top-k CSO candidates with similarity scores.
- `POST /verify` — accepts (label, candidate), returns LLM verification + confidence.

---

## 7. Sources

- [CSO Downloads Portal](https://cso.kmi.open.ac.uk/downloads)
- [The Computer Science Ontology (CSO) — SKM3](https://skm.kmi.open.ac.uk/cso/)
- [CSO v3.4.1 release notes](https://skm.kmi.open.ac.uk/computer-science-ontology-v3-4-1/)
- [The Computer Science Ontology paper (Data Intelligence, MIT Press)](https://direct.mit.edu/dint/article/2/3/379/94891/The-Computer-Science-Ontology-A-Comprehensive)
- [EVōC GitHub](https://github.com/TutteInstitute/evoc)
- [evoc PyPI](https://pypi.org/project/evoc/)
- [OLIVE: Ontology Learning With Integrated Vector Embeddings (Sage 2025)](https://journals.sagepub.com/doi/10.1177/15705838251329268)
- [Ontology Population with LLMs — Asbestos Case Study (Sage 2025)](https://journals.sagepub.com/doi/10.1177/15705838251334528)
- [Ontology Population using LLMs (arXiv 2411.01612)](https://arxiv.org/html/2411.01612v1)
- [MILA — Ontology Matching with LLMs and Prioritized DFS (arXiv 2501.11441)](https://arxiv.org/html/2501.11441v1)
- [GenOM — Ontology Matching with Description Generation (arXiv 2508.10703)](https://arxiv.org/html/2508.10703)
- [LLMs4OL 2025 Challenge Overview](https://www.tib-op.org/ojs/index.php/ocp/article/view/2913)
- [Springer Nature CSO launch announcement](https://group.springernature.com/us/group/media/press-releases/springer-nature-and-the-open-university-launch-a-unique/16386730)

- Available in `.nt`, `.owl`, `.ttl`, `.csv` from <https://cso.kmi.open.ac.uk/downloads>.

### 1.3 Recent expansion (relevant to this thesis)

- **v3.4.1, February 2025:** ~100 new AI topics added — Generative AI, Large Language Models, Retrieval Augmented Generation, etc.
- This release substantially improves coverage for CS-undergraduate AI/ML curriculum content, directly relevant to the thesis demo's planned 6-course program.

### 1.4 Implications for the thesis substrate

- CSO is **SKOS-shaped**, so it can be ingested into Apache Jena Fuseki as a separate named graph and queried via standard SPARQL.
- Ingest cost: one-time bulk load. Approximate triple count is manageable for in-memory Fuseki at the demo scale.
- Custom CSO predicates (`cso:relatedEquivalent`, `cso:contributesTo`) are documented and can be queried alongside SKOS predicates in alignment workflows.
- No conflict with the engine's existing namespace decisions (ADR-005 addendum): CSO lives in its own namespace (`cso:` / `csot:` for topics), imported, not maintained by the engine team.

---

## 2. Clustering Tool — EVōC

### 2.1 Identity

- **EVōC** (Embedding Vector Oriented Clustering), pronounced "evoke."
- Author: Leland McInnes, Tutte Institute for Mathematics and Computing.
- Same lineage as **UMAP** and **HDBSCAN** (same author).

### 2.2 Technical properties

- Combines a UMAP-like node embedding with HDBSCAN-style density estimation and **multi-layer persistence analysis**.
- **Auto-hierarchical:** produces a list of cluster-label vectors at multiple granularities (fine-grained → coarse). No need to specify the number of clusters in advance.
- **Stable:** persistence analysis filters out noise-driven clusters that would not reproduce on slight input perturbation.
- **Duplicate detection:** automatic flagging of duplicate or near-duplicate vectors.
- **API:** scikit-learn–compatible, Python ≥3.10. Latest pip release 2026-02-27.
- **Repo:** <https://github.com/TutteInstitute/evoc>
- **PyPI:** <https://pypi.org/project/evoc/>

### 2.3 Why EVōC fits the thesis pipeline

- The **multi-layer hierarchy** maps naturally onto SKOS broader/narrower relations and onto CSO's own hierarchy. Coarse clusters can correspond to higher-level CSO topics; fine clusters to leaf topics.
- **No `k` specification** matches the thesis spirit: structure emerges from data rather than being prescribed by the author or the engine.
- Author-recognized provenance (UMAP/HDBSCAN lineage) provides a defensible cite for the thesis methodology section.

---

## 3. State of the Art — LLM Ontology Population & Matching (2025)

The pipeline you sketched (cluster → label → search reference ontology → match-or-mint) is an active 2025 research direction. Three representative papers and one shared-task series:

### 3.1 Ontology Population with LLMs (Sage 2025; arXiv 2411.01612)

**Authors:** Sarah Ayad, Lydia Khelifa Chibout

**Pipeline:**
1. **Pre-processing:** input texts (Wikipedia articles, Wikidata TTL, domain records) into TSV triples plus filtered ontology modules.
2. **Text retrieval:** large texts handled via either summarization or RAG retrieval. RAG uses `sentence-transformers/all-MiniLM-L6-v2` embeddings stored in a vector DB (LangChain pipeline). Top-k chunks by cosine similarity.
3. **Population prompt:** few-shot, structured-format examples (`hasAgeValue(Agent, xsd:double): hasAgeValue(Absalom Jones, 71)`). Explicit "skip relations not in text" instruction. Temperature = 0.
4. **Output:** TSV triples, parsed for evaluation.

**Models tested:** GPT-4 and Llama-3.

**Evaluation:** Coverage at ≥80% string-similarity threshold (cosine on TF-IDF, FuzzyWuzzy ratio + token-set ratio, Jaro-Winkler). Best: GPT-4 at 87.87% coverage on Enslaved ontology. Llama-3 max 71.25%.

**Notable absence:** No formal OWL/SKOS axiomatization in LLM output — TSV triples only. Formal axiomatization happens before the LLM step, not as its output.

**Relevance to thesis:** Demonstrates the few-shot prompt-and-parse pattern. Shows GPT-4 quality for entity-attribute extraction. Less relevant for *equivalence matching*, more relevant for *attribute population* of new concepts.

### 3.2 MILA — Ontology Matching with Prioritized Depth-First Search (arXiv 2501.11441)

**Pipeline:** Embeds a "retrieve-identify-prompt" loop within a **prioritized depth-first search** over a bidirectional source/target search tree (up to four levels deep).

**Embedding:** **SBERT `multi-qa-distilbert-cos-v1`** to encode preprocessed entity labels.

**Retrieval:**
- Top-k = 5 candidates per source entity by cosine similarity.
- Confidence threshold: **0.75** (below threshold candidates discarded).
- Scoring rounded to 5 decimal places.

**LLM verification:** **LlaMA-3.1 70B** at default temperature (0.7), zero-shot binary-decision prompt:

> "You are a helpful expert in ontology matching...Classify if the following concepts are equivalent: Source concept: [name] Target concept: [name]...answer 'Yes'...or 'No'."

Prompt includes ontology names and semantic types; **excludes definitions and hierarchical context**.

**Scoring function:**

```
f(e_source, e_target) = max({score(x,y) | x ∈ synonyms(e_source), y ∈ synonyms(e_target)})
```

**Match selection logic:**
- High-confidence: bidirectional first-ranked correspondence (both entities are top match for each other).
- Low-confidence: present but not first-ranked → escalate to LLM verification.

**Output:** Pairwise equivalence correspondences. Paper does **not** explicitly emit SKOS predicates (`exactMatch`, `closeMatch`); reports raw equivalence pairs.

**Evaluation results (F-Measure, unsupervised):**
- OMIM-ORDO: **0.831** (+17% over LogMapBio)
- NCIT-DOID: **0.948** (+3% over HybridOM)
- SNOMED-FMA: **0.894** (+13% over BERTMap / HybridOM)
- SNOMED-NCIT Neoplasm: **0.903** (+17% over LogMapBio)

**Computational efficiency:** MILA reduces LLM calls by **92–98%** vs baseline RAG (e.g., 375 vs 23,430 prompts on NCIT-DOID).

**Relevance to thesis:** This is the closest match to the alignment phase of the proposed thesis pipeline. The retrieve-then-prompt + embedding-similarity-threshold + LLM-binary-verify pattern is directly transferable. Use as a citation anchor for the alignment methodology.

### 3.3 GenOM — Ontology Matching with Description Generation (arXiv 2508.10703)

**Distinguishing innovation:** Generates **textual definitions** to enrich sparse ontology metadata before matching.

**Pipeline:**
1. **Description generation:** Qwen2.5-7B prompted with concept labels + synonyms + parent concepts + verbalized axioms, producing concise definitions designed to be "semantically precise, distinguishable from related terms."
2. **Embedding:** `text-embedding-3-small` encodes (label + synonyms + generated definition).
3. **Retrieval:** HNSW indexing returns top-10 candidates per source concept.
4. **LLM judgment:** Qwen2.5-32B performs binary YES/NO classification. Extracts **token-level probability** as confidence:

```
P(YES) = softmax(z_YES) / (softmax(z_YES) + softmax(z_NO))
```

5. **Filtering:** Dual thresholds — `λ_prob` for LLM confidence, `λ_cs` for cosine similarity. Pairs not exceeding both are discarded.
6. **Post-processing:** Merge with exact-matching baselines (LogMapLt, BERTMapLt) for precision.

**Output:** Equivalence mappings only. Subsumption explicitly out of scope.

**Computational cost:** HNSW for sublinear retrieval. Lightweight token-level scoring (no full natural-language justification). Demonstrated on biomedical ontologies up to ~89K concepts.

**No mint behavior:** Concepts that fail to match are *discarded*, not minted as new nodes. This is a gap relative to the thesis vision.

**Relevance to thesis:** Provides the **definition-augmentation** technique — useful when CSO concepts have sparse metadata. The token-level confidence extraction is also a transferable trick. The lack of "mint new concept" handling is a *gap the thesis can fill* — a small but real research contribution.

### 3.4 LLMs4OL Challenge (2nd edition, 2025)

**Format:** Shared task / benchmark series for LLM-based ontology learning.

**2025 emphasis:** Hybrid embedding+LLM architectures dominate participant submissions, especially for taxonomy discovery sub-tasks.

**Benchmark availability:** Provides standardized eval datasets and metrics. Useful as a comparison point if the thesis pipeline is ever benchmarked against published systems.

**Reference:** <https://www.tib-op.org/ojs/index.php/ocp/article/view/2913>

**Relevance to thesis:** Establishes that the proposed thesis pipeline operates within a recognized evaluation framework. Useful citation for thesis's "evaluation strategy" section.

---

## 4. Pipeline Patterns Observed Across the Literature

Synthesizing the three papers and the LLMs4OL challenge:

### 4.1 The retrieve-then-prompt pattern is canonical (2025)

All competitive 2025 systems share a two-stage architecture:

1. **Embedding-based retrieval** narrows the candidate space (top-k by cosine similarity, threshold-filtered).
2. **LLM-based verification** decides equivalence on retrieved candidates.

This is dramatically cheaper than naive all-pairs LLM comparison (MILA reports 92–98% LLM-call reduction).

### 4.2 SBERT-class embeddings dominate

`sentence-transformers/all-MiniLM-L6-v2`, `multi-qa-distilbert-cos-v1`, and `text-embedding-3-small` all show up across the recent papers. All are SBERT-family or OpenAI's general-purpose embedding API. The thesis can pick any without controversy; `all-MiniLM-L6-v2` is the most-cited free option.

### 4.3 Confidence scoring varies, threshold filtering is universal

- MILA: cosine threshold 0.75, top-1 bidirectional.
- GenOM: dual thresholds (cosine + LLM-token-probability).
- OLIVE / similar: 80% string-similarity coverage.

The thesis pipeline must commit to a thresholding strategy. Token-level LLM probability (GenOM) is the cleanest signal; binary YES/NO with retry (MILA) is simpler to implement.

### 4.4 SKOS predicate emission is underspecified in the literature

Most papers report raw equivalence pairs without committing to `skos:exactMatch` vs `skos:closeMatch`. This is a small gap the thesis can fill cleanly: emit `skos:exactMatch` for high-confidence (e.g., LLM probability ≥0.95), `skos:closeMatch` for moderate (0.75 ≤ p < 0.95), `skos:relatedMatch` or no edge below.

### 4.5 No-match handling is a research gap

GenOM discards. MILA doesn't address. OLIVE doesn't address. The thesis vision — **mint new concepts when no reference match exists** — is novel relative to the surveyed papers. This becomes a defensible thesis contribution.

---

## 5. Implications for the Thesis Demo

### 5.1 The pipeline is well-grounded

The user-sketched pipeline (cluster → label → match-or-mint) is **not speculative**. It matches 2025 SOTA almost step-for-step, with one genuine novel element (no-match minting).

### 5.2 Substrate impact is minimal

- **No new substrate types** (`knl:` does not grow). All emitted predicates are SKOS-standard.
- **CSO ingested as a named graph in Fuseki** alongside the user's authored graph.
- **Alignment edges** (`skos:exactMatch` / `skos:closeMatch` / `skos:relatedMatch`) live in the user's graph between user concepts and CSO concepts.
- **Auto-minted concepts** live in the user's namespace (e.g., `cs:auto_concept_42`) with provenance metadata recording the cluster and pipeline version.
- **No `kn:traversal_role` or other new substrate vocabulary needed.**

### 5.3 The four-layer namespace architecture (ADR-005 addendum) holds

| Layer | Role in pipeline |
|---|---|
| `kn:` | Substrate kernel — unchanged |
| `knl:` | Engine-required edge types — unchanged, no growth |
| External (`cso:`, `skos:`, `bibo:`) | CSO + SKOS imported as separate named graphs |
| User namespace | User-authored content + auto-minted concepts + alignment edges |

Pipeline integration does **not** require revising namespace decisions.

### 5.4 Scope options for thesis (revised with research)

| Scope | Effort | Thesis claim strength | Research novelty |
|---|---|---|---|
| **(A) Full pipeline** — EVōC + LLM labels + CSO retrieve-then-prompt + mint-on-no-match + alignment edges + UI overlay | 2–3 months | Strong | Mint-on-no-match is novel; rest is replication of 2025 SOTA in a new application context |
| **(A-lite)** — As (A) but with a small CSO subset (~500 concepts), single prompt template, manual review of alignment outputs as part of demo | 6–8 weeks | Strong | Same as (A); the curated subset is honest about scope |
| **(B) Grounding only** — preload CSO, hand-author SKOS alignment edges as demo, skip EVōC/LLM | 2–3 weeks | Moderate | Demonstrates substrate handles SKOS interop; no learning contribution |
| **(C) EVōC only** — clusters as visual grouping, no ontology grounding | 2–3 weeks | Weak | Misses the "grounded in research ontology" insight |

**Recommended scope:** **(A-lite)** for the thesis demo timeline. Defends the strongest claim within a realistic 6–8 week window. The "small CSO subset" can be justified by documenting filtering criteria (e.g., "topics relevant to undergraduate CS curriculum, intersection of CSO with the demo's 6 courses").

### 5.5 What ADR-007 should now record

Original framing: "Should there be a Category type in the substrate?"

Revised framing post-research: ADR-007 records two coupled decisions:

1. **No `Category` substrate type.** Categories are emergent, not authored.
2. **EVōC + CSO grounding pipeline is adopted as the categorization mechanism.** Scope is (A-lite). SKOS predicates emit alignment edges. New concepts mint in user namespace. No substrate-vocabulary additions.

ADR-007 should also:

- Cite the four 2025 papers (OLIVE / Ontology Population, MILA, GenOM, LLMs4OL) as state-of-the-art context.
- Identify the no-match-mint behavior as the thesis's incremental contribution over surveyed work.
- Document the namespace impact (none — addendum stands).
- Defer the EVōC-API-contract and prompt-template details to a follow-up implementation ADR.

---

## 6. Open Questions

These should be settled before drafting ADR-007:

### 6.1 Scope commitment

(A-lite) is the recommended scope, but the thesis advisor / committee may prefer (B) or (C) for risk reasons. **Decide:** is the pipeline a thesis-required deliverable or a future-work demonstration?

### 6.2 Embedding model choice

`sentence-transformers/all-MiniLM-L6-v2` is the safest cite. Decide whether to use that or a more recent model (`text-embedding-3-small`, `bge-small-en-v1.5`, etc.). Trade-off: cite stability vs. quality.

### 6.3 LLM choice

GPT-4 (highest quality, paid API), Qwen2.5-32B (open-weights, good quality, MIT-license-equivalent), Llama-3.1 70B (open-weights, large model). Decide based on cost and reproducibility for the thesis defense.

### 6.4 Threshold strategy

Token-probability-based (GenOM) requires API support (OpenAI logprobs, vLLM). Binary YES/NO (MILA) works on any chat-completion API. Decide based on chosen LLM API.

### 6.5 SKOS predicate mapping policy

A concrete proposal:

- LLM confidence ≥0.95 AND cosine ≥0.85 → `skos:exactMatch`
- LLM confidence ≥0.80 AND cosine ≥0.75 → `skos:closeMatch`
- Below thresholds → `skos:relatedMatch` (if cluster shares ≥1 high-similarity ancestor in CSO) or **mint**.

Confirm thresholds with pilot tests before locking in ADR-007.

### 6.6 No-match mint provenance schema

Auto-minted concepts need provenance:

```turtle
cs:auto_concept_42
    rdf:type            knl:Concept ;        # or skos:Concept
    rdfs:label          "[LLM-generated label]" ;
    prov:wasGeneratedBy cs:evoc_pipeline_run_2026_05_03 ;
    prov:wasDerivedFrom cs:cluster_42 ;
    skos:relatedMatch   cso:nearest_concept .  # if soft anchor exists
```

Confirm provenance vocab choice (PROV-O is standard; lighter alternative is just custom predicates).

### 6.7 EVōC service API contract

Defer to a separate implementation ADR. Note that the pipeline assumes a stable API:

- `POST /cluster` — accepts list of node URIs + content, returns cluster assignments and hierarchy.
- `POST /label` — accepts cluster, returns LLM-generated label + confidence.
- `POST /align` — accepts label, returns top-k CSO candidates with similarity scores.
- `POST /verify` — accepts (label, candidate), returns LLM verification + confidence.

---

## 7. Sources

- [The Computer Science Ontology (CSO) — SKM3](https://skm.kmi.open.ac.uk/cso/)

# ADR-007: EVōC + CSO Categorization Pipeline

**Status:** Accepted
**Date:** 2026-04-28
**Deciders:** Shizhong Yu
**Related:** ADR-003 (reflexivity foundation), ADR-005 (`kn:` scope under Reading A; namespace architecture addendum), VISION.md (§4.8 reflexive substrate, §6 v1 scope)
**Builds on:** ADR-005 namespace architecture addendum

---

## Context

The original queued question — "Should the substrate include a `Category` type for grouping concepts?" — was reframed during the post-Stage-5 reconciliation. Categories are *not* an authored substrate type. They are *emergent groupings* discovered from authored content by a clustering pipeline, optionally aligned to canonical research ontologies.

This converts the question from "design a `Category` vocabulary" into "design an integration pipeline that produces and grounds emergent categories."

A literature scan covering CSO (Computer Science Ontology), EVōC (Tutte Institute clustering library), and 2025 SOTA LLM ontology-population/matching papers (MILA, GenOM, OLIVE, LLMs4OL Challenge) confirms that the pipeline outlined below is well-grounded and that the thesis demo can claim a small but real novel contribution.

The full literature digest is captured in the Masters thesis Draft 2 notes folder: `evoc-cso-ontology-grounding-pipeline.md`. This ADR records only the design decisions derived from that research.

---

## Decisions

### D1 — No `Category` type in the substrate

The substrate does not gain a `knl:Category` (or equivalent) class. Categories are not user-authored, and the namespace architecture established in ADR-005's addendum stands unchanged.

### D2 — EVōC + CSO grounding pipeline as the categorization mechanism

The thesis demo adopts a five-stage pipeline:

1. **Clustering.** EVōC clusters authored-node text embeddings. Multi-layer hierarchy emerges automatically.
2. **Labeling.** LLM generates a semantic label for each cluster (zero-shot prompt over the cluster's representative members).
3. **Retrieve-then-prompt grounding.** Cluster labels are embedded with SBERT-class embeddings, retrieved against a CSO concept index by cosine similarity, and verified by an LLM binary-decision prompt.
4. **Alignment emission.** Successful matches emit SKOS predicates between the user-authored cluster and the CSO concept (see D4).
5. **Mint-on-no-match.** Clusters with no acceptable CSO match are minted as new concepts in the user namespace, with PROV-O provenance recording the cluster origin (see D5).

This pattern matches 2025 SOTA in stages 1–4 (MILA, GenOM, OLIVE). Stage 5 — minting on no-match — is novel relative to the surveyed papers (which discard unmapped candidates) and is the thesis's incremental contribution to the literature.

### D3 — Scope is (A-lite)

Implementation target for the thesis demo:

- Full pipeline implemented end-to-end.
- **Curated CSO subset** (~500 concepts relevant to undergraduate CS curriculum), not the full ~14K-concept ontology.
- Single prompt template for label generation; single template for verification. No prompt-engineering experimentation in v1.
- Manual review of alignment outputs as part of the live demo, demonstrating both successful matches and mint cases.
- Implementation window: 6–8 weeks.

Rejected alternatives:

- **(A) Full pipeline + full CSO + multi-prompt experimentation** — out of timeline.
- **(B) Grounding only** (preload CSO, hand-author alignments) — discards EVōC and LLM contributions.
- **(C) Clusters-only** (visual overlay, no ontology grounding) — loses the "grounded in research ontology" insight that motivates the pipeline.

### D4 — SKOS predicates for alignment edges

Alignment edges between user-authored cluster concepts and CSO concepts use standard SKOS predicates with confidence-tier mapping:

| Confidence tier | LLM probability | Cosine similarity | Predicate emitted |
|---|---|---|---|
| High | ≥ 0.95 | ≥ 0.85 | `skos:exactMatch` |
| Moderate | ≥ 0.80 | ≥ 0.75 | `skos:closeMatch` |
| Low (soft anchor) | ≥ 0.60 | ≥ 0.60 | `skos:relatedMatch` |
| Below all | — | — | mint (see D5) |

Thresholds are starting values. Final thresholds will be locked after pilot evaluation against the demo curriculum content.

### D5 — Mint-on-no-match with PROV-O provenance

Clusters that fail to match any CSO concept above the lowest confidence tier mint a new concept node in the user namespace.

Mint schema:

```turtle
cs:auto_concept_42
    rdf:type             skos:Concept ;
    rdfs:label           "Embedding-derived label" ;
    prov:wasGeneratedBy  cs:evoc_pipeline_run_2026_05_03 ;
    prov:wasDerivedFrom  cs:cluster_42 ;
    skos:relatedMatch    cso:nearest_concept .   # only if a soft anchor was found
```

- Lives in the user namespace (e.g., `cs:` for the demo curriculum).
- Typed as `skos:Concept` directly (consistent with ADR-005 namespace addendum: external ontology predicates over inventing `knl:`).
- Provenance vocabulary is **PROV-O** (W3C standard). No custom provenance predicates introduced.

### D6 — Zero substrate-vocabulary additions

This ADR adds zero `kn:` or `knl:` symbols. Every emitted predicate is SKOS-standard or PROV-O-standard. ADR-005's namespace architecture addendum is unchanged.

---

## Consequences

### Positive

- **Substrate stays small.** No growth in `kn:` or `knl:` from this work.
- **Thesis claim grounded in 2025 SOTA.** MILA, GenOM, and OLIVE provide direct citations for the retrieve-then-prompt and embedding+LLM-verification pattern. The mint-on-no-match step is a defensible novel contribution.
- **Research-canonical anchors automatic.** Demo concepts get linked to CSO without manual curation, demonstrating substrate readiness for ontology interop.
- **Pipeline iterates independently.** EVōC service and prompt templates can evolve without substrate changes.
- **Defensible scope window.** 6–8 weeks is realistic for the thesis defense timeline.

### Negative

- **Non-trivial implementation.** Clustering, embedding, LLM integration, prompt engineering, threshold tuning, and evaluation are all part of v1 work.
- **External LLM dependency.** Whatever LLM is chosen introduces cost, rate limits, and reproducibility considerations for the thesis defense.
- **Threshold tuning requires pilot data.** Demo curriculum content may not exist at full volume when thresholds need to be locked.
- **CSO subset curation bias.** The chosen ~500-concept subset must be documented (selection criteria, audit trail) to defend against arbitrary-cherry-pick concerns.

### Neutral

- This ADR supersedes the original "Category type ADR" framing entirely. The original framing's open questions (SKOS-vs-invent, hierarchy modeling, taxonomic structure) are no longer relevant — they were artifacts of treating categories as substrate.
- Future versions can swap reference ontologies (ACM CCS, schema.org, domain-specific) without substrate changes. The pipeline is parameterized by reference-ontology choice, not the substrate.

---

## Companion Work

1. **EVōC service API contract ADR.** Stable HTTP contract between the C# backend and the Python FastAPI EVōC service. Endpoints: `cluster`, `label`, `align`, `verify`. Schema, error semantics, idempotency.
2. **Pilot evaluation.** Small-curriculum pilot validates threshold values from D4. Results inform final threshold lock and any tier-mapping adjustments.
3. **CSO subset selection criteria.** Documented filter logic (proposal: "intersect CSO topics with curriculum keyword vocabulary; expand by one hop in CSO `skos:broaderGeneric` hierarchy").
4. **Provenance schema confirmation.** Confirm PROV-O is sufficient. Mint-specific custom predicates added only if PROV-O cannot express something needed.
5. **Update `THESIS_DEMO_GAP_ANALYSIS.md`.** Mark categorization as "implemented via EVōC + CSO pipeline, not as substrate type."

---

## Open Questions

### LLM choice

Trade-offs: GPT-4 (paid, highest quality, supports logprobs API for D4), Qwen2.5-32B (open-weights, MIT-license-equivalent, supports logprobs via vLLM), Llama-3.1 70B (open-weights, large model). Decision drivers: cost ceiling, reproducibility for thesis defense, support for token-level probability extraction (needed by D4 threshold strategy).

### Embedding model

Trade-offs: `sentence-transformers/all-MiniLM-L6-v2` (most-cited free option, 2025 papers default), `text-embedding-3-small` (OpenAI, paid, higher quality), `bge-small-en-v1.5` (newer free option, competitive quality). Cite stability vs raw quality.

### Threshold-strategy implementation

Token-probability scoring (GenOM style) requires LLM API support for logprobs (OpenAI, vLLM, llama.cpp grammar mode, etc.). Binary YES/NO scoring (MILA style) works on any chat-completion API but is a coarser signal. Trade-off: implementation simplicity vs signal quality.

### Mint provenance granularity

Per-pipeline-run record (one provenance node, all minted concepts derive from it) is simpler. Per-mint-event record (one provenance node per minted concept, with timestamp and per-event confidence) is more queryable. Decision affects PROV-O usage pattern.

### CSO subset selection method

Hand-curated (highest quality, lowest reproducibility) vs algorithmic filter (defensible criteria, may miss curriculum-specific concepts). Likely hybrid: algorithmic filter + manual review pass.

---

# ADR-007: EVōC + CSO Categorization Pipeline

**Status:** Accepted
**Date:** 2026-04-28
**Deciders:** Shizhong Yu
**Related:** ADR-003 (reflexivity foundation), ADR-005 (`kn:` scope under Reading A; namespace architecture addendum), VISION.md (§4.8 reflexive substrate, §6 v1 scope)
**Builds on:** ADR-005 namespace architecture addendum

---

## Context

The original queued question — "Should the substrate include a `Category` type for grouping concepts?" — was reframed during the post-Stage-5 reconciliation. Categories are *not* an authored substrate type. They are *emergent groupings* discovered from authored content by a clustering pipeline, optionally aligned to canonical research ontologies.

This converts the question from "design a `Category` vocabulary" into "design an integration pipeline that produces and grounds emergent categories."

A literature scan covering CSO (Computer Science Ontology), EVōC (Tutte Institute clustering library), and 2025 SOTA LLM ontology-population/matching papers (MILA, GenOM, OLIVE, LLMs4OL Challenge) confirms that the pipeline outlined below is well-grounded and that the thesis demo can claim a small but real novel contribution.

The full literature digest is captured in the Masters thesis Draft 2 notes folder: `evoc-cso-ontology-grounding-pipeline.md`. This ADR records only the design decisions derived from that research.

---

## Decisions

### D1 — No `Category` type in the substrate

The substrate does not gain a `knl:Category` (or equivalent) class. Categories are not user-authored, and the namespace architecture established in ADR-005's addendum stands unchanged.

### D2 — EVōC + CSO grounding pipeline as the categorization mechanism

The thesis demo adopts a five-stage pipeline:

1. **Clustering.** EVōC clusters authored-node text embeddings. Multi-layer hierarchy emerges automatically.
2. **Labeling.** LLM generates a semantic label for each cluster (zero-shot prompt over the cluster's representative members).
3. **Retrieve-then-prompt grounding.** Cluster labels are embedded with SBERT-class embeddings, retrieved against a CSO concept index by cosine similarity, and verified by an LLM binary-decision prompt.
4. **Alignment emission.** Successful matches emit SKOS predicates between the user-authored cluster and the CSO concept (see D4).
5. **Mint-on-no-match.** Clusters with no acceptable CSO match are minted as new concepts in the user namespace, with PROV-O provenance recording the cluster origin (see D5).

This pattern matches 2025 SOTA in stages 1–4 (MILA, GenOM, OLIVE). Stage 5 — minting on no-match — is novel relative to the surveyed papers (which discard unmapped candidates) and is the thesis's incremental contribution to the literature.

### D3 — Scope is (A-lite)

Implementation target for the thesis demo:

- Full pipeline implemented end-to-end.
- **Curated CSO subset** (~500 concepts relevant to undergraduate CS curriculum), not the full ~14K-concept ontology.
- Single prompt template for label generation; single template for verification. No prompt-engineering experimentation in v1.
- Manual review of alignment outputs as part of the live demo, demonstrating both successful matches and mint cases.
- Implementation window: 6–8 weeks.

Rejected alternatives:

- **(A) Full pipeline + full CSO + multi-prompt experimentation** — out of timeline.
- **(B) Grounding only** (preload CSO, hand-author alignments) — discards EVōC and LLM contributions.
- **(C) Clusters-only** (visual overlay, no ontology grounding) — loses the "grounded in research ontology" insight that motivates the pipeline.

### D4 — SKOS predicates for alignment edges

Alignment edges between user-authored cluster concepts and CSO concepts use standard SKOS predicates with confidence-tier mapping:

| Confidence tier | LLM probability | Cosine similarity | Predicate emitted |
|---|---|---|---|
| High | ≥ 0.95 | ≥ 0.85 | `skos:exactMatch` |
| Moderate | ≥ 0.80 | ≥ 0.75 | `skos:closeMatch` |
| Low (soft anchor) | ≥ 0.60 | ≥ 0.60 | `skos:relatedMatch` |
| Below all | — | — | mint (see D5) |

Thresholds are starting values. Final thresholds will be locked after pilot evaluation against the demo curriculum content.

### D5 — Mint-on-no-match with PROV-O provenance

Clusters that fail to match any CSO concept above the lowest confidence tier mint a new concept node in the user namespace.

Mint schema:

```turtle
cs:auto_concept_42
    rdf:type             skos:Concept ;
    rdfs:label           "Embedding-derived label" ;
    prov:wasGeneratedBy  cs:evoc_pipeline_run_2026_05_03 ;
    prov:wasDerivedFrom  cs:cluster_42 ;
    skos:relatedMatch    cso:nearest_concept .   # only if a soft anchor was found
```

- Lives in the user namespace (e.g., `cs:` for the demo curriculum).
- Typed as `skos:Concept` directly (consistent with ADR-005 namespace addendum: external ontology predicates over inventing `knl:`).
- Provenance vocabulary is **PROV-O** (W3C standard). No custom provenance predicates introduced.

### D6 — Zero substrate-vocabulary additions

This ADR adds zero `kn:` or `knl:` symbols. Every emitted predicate is SKOS-standard or PROV-O-standard. ADR-005's namespace architecture addendum is unchanged.

---

## Consequences

### Positive

- **Substrate stays small.** No growth in `kn:` or `knl:` from this work.
- **Thesis claim grounded in 2025 SOTA.** MILA, GenOM, and OLIVE provide direct citations for the retrieve-then-prompt and embedding+LLM-verification pattern. The mint-on-no-match step is a defensible novel contribution.
- **Research-canonical anchors automatic.** Demo concepts get linked to CSO without manual curation, demonstrating substrate readiness for ontology interop.
- **Pipeline iterates independently.** EVōC service and prompt templates can evolve without substrate changes.
- **Defensible scope window.** 6–8 weeks is realistic for the thesis defense timeline.

### Negative

- **Non-trivial implementation.** Clustering, embedding, LLM integration, prompt engineering, threshold tuning, and evaluation are all part of v1 work.
- **External LLM dependency.** Whatever LLM is chosen introduces cost, rate limits, and reproducibility considerations for the thesis defense.
- **Threshold tuning requires pilot data.** Demo curriculum content may not exist at full volume when thresholds need to be locked.
- **CSO subset curation bias.** The chosen ~500-concept subset must be documented (selection criteria, audit trail) to defend against arbitrary-cherry-pick concerns.

### Neutral

- This ADR supersedes the original "Category type ADR" framing entirely. The original framing's open questions (SKOS-vs-invent, hierarchy modeling, taxonomic structure) are no longer relevant — they were artifacts of treating categories as substrate.
- Future versions can swap reference ontologies (ACM CCS, schema.org, domain-specific) without substrate changes. The pipeline is parameterized by reference-ontology choice, not the substrate.

---

## Companion Work

1. **EVōC service API contract ADR.** Stable HTTP contract between the C# backend and the Python FastAPI EVōC service. Endpoints: `cluster`, `label`, `align`, `verify`. Schema, error semantics, idempotency.
2. **Pilot evaluation.** Small-curriculum pilot validates threshold values from D4. Results inform final threshold lock and any tier-mapping adjustments.
3. **CSO subset selection criteria.** Documented filter logic (proposal: "intersect CSO topics with curriculum keyword vocabulary; expand by one hop in CSO `skos:broaderGeneric` hierarchy").
4. **Provenance schema confirmation.** Confirm PROV-O is sufficient. Mint-specific custom predicates added only if PROV-O cannot express something needed.
5. **Update `THESIS_DEMO_GAP_ANALYSIS.md`.** Mark categorization as "implemented via EVōC + CSO pipeline, not as substrate type."

---

## Open Questions

### LLM choice

Trade-offs: GPT-4 (paid, highest quality, supports logprobs API for D4), Qwen2.5-32B (open-weights, MIT-license-equivalent, supports logprobs via vLLM), Llama-3.1 70B (open-weights, large model). Decision drivers: cost ceiling, reproducibility for thesis defense, support for token-level probability extraction (needed by D4 threshold strategy).

### Embedding model

Trade-offs: `sentence-transformers/all-MiniLM-L6-v2` (most-cited free option, 2025 papers default), `text-embedding-3-small` (OpenAI, paid, higher quality), `bge-small-en-v1.5` (newer free option, competitive quality). Cite stability vs raw quality.

### Threshold-strategy implementation

Token-probability scoring (GenOM style) requires LLM API support for logprobs (OpenAI, vLLM, llama.cpp grammar mode, etc.). Binary YES/NO scoring (MILA style) works on any chat-completion API but is a coarser signal. Trade-off: implementation simplicity vs signal quality.

### Mint provenance granularity

Per-pipeline-run record (one provenance node, all minted concepts derive from it) is simpler. Per-mint-event record (one provenance node per minted concept, with timestamp and per-event confidence) is more queryable. Decision affects PROV-O usage pattern.

### CSO subset selection method

Hand-curated (highest quality, lowest reproducibility) vs algorithmic filter (defensible criteria, may miss curriculum-specific concepts). Likely hybrid: algorithmic filter + manual review pass.

---

## References

- **Research note:** `evoc-cso-ontology-grounding-pipeline.md` (Thesis Draft 2 Notes folder) — full literature digest informing this ADR.
- **ADR-003** — Reflexivity as foundation.
- **ADR-005** — `kn:` scope under Reading A; namespace architecture addendum.
- **VISION.md** §4.8 (reflexive substrate), §6 (v1 scope).
- **MILA** — Ontology Matching with LLMs and Prioritized Depth-First Search (arXiv 2501.11441).
- **GenOM** — Ontology Matching with Description Generation and LLM (arXiv 2508.10703).
- **OLIVE** — Ontology Learning With Integrated Vector Embeddings (Sage 2025).
- **LLMs4OL Challenge 2025** — 2nd Large Language Models for Ontology Learning Challenge (tib-op.org/ojs).
- **CSO** — Computer Science Ontology v3.4.1 downloads (cso.kmi.open.ac.uk/downloads).
- **EVōC** — Tutte Institute clustering library (github.com/TutteInstitute/evoc).
